lesson.title: Beyond the Eyeball: Calculating the Best-Fit Line with Linear Regression
lesson.summary: Linear regression replaces the guesswork of eyeballing a trend line with a precise formula that finds the one line minimizing the total squared distance to every data point.
lesson.body:
The line of best fit you just learned to sketch by eye has a real weakness: it is subjective. Two people looking at the same scatterplot can draw two different lines that both look reasonable, and get two different equations. Linear regression fixes this by replacing the sketch with a calculation, so that everyone who runs the same numbers on the same data gets exactly the same line.

The key idea is called least squares. For any candidate line, compare each data point's actual y-value to the y-value the line predicts at that x. The difference, actual minus predicted, is called a residual. Some residuals are positive, because the point sits above the line, and some are negative, because the point sits below it. If you square every residual, all the values become positive, so they cannot cancel each other out, and larger misses get penalized much more heavily than small ones. The regression line, sometimes called the least-squares line, is defined as the one specific line that makes the sum of all these squared residuals as small as possible.

For a data set of points, the slope and y-intercept of the least-squares line can be found with these formulas, where x-bar and y-bar are the mean of the x-values and the mean of the y-values:

slope m equals the sum of (x minus x-bar) times (y minus y-bar), divided by the sum of (x minus x-bar) squared
intercept b equals y-bar minus m times x-bar

Unlike the by-eye method, which only uses two points, these formulas pull in every single data point, so no point is ignored.

Worked example, using the same five students from the line of best fit lesson:

Hours studied (x): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Quiz score (y): 3, 5, 4, 8, 10

First find the means: x-bar = (1+2+3+4+5)/5 = 15/5 = 3, and y-bar = (3+5+4+8+10)/5 = 30/5 = 6. Next, for each point, find how far x is from x-bar and how far y is from y-bar, and multiply those two differences together:

x = 1: (1 - 3) = -2, (3 - 6) = -3, product = 6
x = 2: (2 - 3) = -1, (5 - 6) = -1, product = 1
x = 3: (3 - 3) = 0, (4 - 6) = -2, product = 0
x = 4: (4 - 3) = 1, (8 - 6) = 2, product = 2
x = 5: (5 - 3) = 2, (10 - 6) = 4, product = 8

The sum of these products is 6 + 1 + 0 + 2 + 8 = 17. The sum of the squared x-differences is 4 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 4 = 10. So the slope is m = 17/10 = 1.7, and the intercept is b = 6 - 1.7(3) = 6 - 5.1 = 0.9. The regression line is y = 1.7x + 0.9.

Compare this to the by-eye line from the previous lesson, y = 1.75x + 1.25. They are close, but not the same, and the regression line is provably better in the least-squares sense. Adding up the squared residuals for the regression line gives 0.16 + 0.49 + 4.00 + 0.09 + 0.36 = 5.10. Doing the same for the by-eye line gives 0.00 + 0.0625 + 6.25 + 0.0625 + 0.00 = 6.375. The regression line's total squared error, 5.10, is smaller than the by-eye line's, 6.375, which is exactly what least squares promises: no other straight line through this data can produce a smaller sum of squared residuals than the regression line.

Once you have the regression equation, you can use it to predict. A prediction for an x-value inside your original range, called interpolation, tends to be reliable. For example, at x = 3.5 hours, the model predicts y = 1.7(3.5) + 0.9 = 5.95 + 0.9 = 6.85 points, a reasonable estimate since it sits between data you already collected. Predicting outside your original range, called extrapolation, is riskier. At x = 6 hours, the model predicts y = 1.7(6) + 0.9 = 10.2 + 0.9 = 11.1 points, but the quiz only had 10 points possible, so this prediction cannot actually be correct. That contradiction is a useful warning sign, trends observed over a limited range of data are not guaranteed to continue past the edges of that range.

In practice, graphing calculators and computer software calculate regression lines for you instantly, along with the correlation coefficient r you met earlier, which measures how tightly the points cluster around the line. But understanding what is happening underneath, minimizing the sum of squared residuals across every point, is what lets you interpret a regression result correctly instead of trusting it blindly.
